newsitem.title: USA: Mainers rally to defend favorite cracker.
newsitem.headline: Mainers rally to defend favorite cracker.

text.p: CHEBEAGUE ISLAND, Maine - On the coast of Maine, they take chowder crackers seriously. So seriously that international food giant RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. may reverse a decision to eliminate a 204-year-old cracker brand.
Pinched by cookie price wars, Nabisco eliminated about 300 less profitable products in June, including Crown Pilot crackers -- which were sold only in Maine, New Hampshire and Massachusetts.

Now that it has been hit by a barrage of complaints, Nabisco is wondering if it closed the box a bit too soon on its oldest product line. A decision may come in the next few days, a company official said.

"Nabisco is a responsive company. We have been hearing from people in the New England area ... and I can tell you at this point we are definitely considering bringing it back to market," said Ann Smith, Nabisco's director of marketing communications.

The people who live on Chebeague Island about 15 miles north of Portland in Casco Bay first learned trouble was brewing when the island's lone grocery store had trouble restocking. Hopes that the shortage was temporary were dashed with a call to Nabisco's headquarters.

"I was shocked because they had always been around," said Donna Damon, a lifetime island resident who has led the charge to bring back the cracker by encouraging others to complain to Nabisco's toll-free consumer line.
Why would a cracker inspire such loyalty on this island of 375 year-round residents?
"The taste of them, I guess," said Ellsworth Miller -- his answer delivered with the famous, dry accent Mainers use when reminding "people from away" of the stupidity of such questions.

Others contend tradition also is at stake. The recipe used to make Crown Pilots can be traced back 204 years, having been developed by one of the bakeries that was merged to create Nabisco, or the National Biscuit Co.

Stories abound on the Chebeague Island about residents who never went on vacation without taking Crown Pilots with them. People also talk of mailing the crackers to loved ones who moved away from Maine.

The crackers are not merely for eating with bowls of hot fish chowder or clam chowder. Some chowder chefs add crackers to the mixture as it cooks. Others favour a meal of crumbled crackers and salt cod in milk.
"One of our neighbours up the road ... until the Crown Pilot disappeared, he was still having crackers, milk and salt fish every Sunday night," Damon said. "He's just beside himself."
A national television report on the plight of Crown Pilot fans has brought in suggestions for alternative crackers from as far away as Alaska. They have not quite measured up to the original.
Island grocery store owner Ed Doughty tried a brand of crackers from Massachusetts as an alternative to Crown Pilots. "They were good but it was not quite as good," he said.

Damon believes fans of Crown Pilots have provided Nabisco with a ready-made marketing campaign if it changes its mind. She is even considering compiling a cookbook of popular ways to use the crackers.
Smith maintains Nabisco was not surprised by the protest and was "warmed" by the level of response it has received. She said a decision on whether to revive Crown Pilot production will be made soon.
Until then, the women gathered for the regular knitting meeting of the Chebeague Island Ladies Aid Society will continue to discuss Nabisco's actions.

"You see they get rid of the pilot cracker and go to these trendy crackers that will only last a couple a months anyway," said Ellen, who joked that she could only give her first name because she had the island's last unopened box.
